text:
Clear and cold as the evening settles in. The sun set at 4:17 under a clean sky, and we're at 28 now with hardly any wind. Tonight stays quiet with a low around 23, so expect frost on the windshield first thing.

Thanksgiving looks like a dry day for the most part. It starts with some sun, then the clouds thicken by afternoon, and the high lands near 42. One model runs warmer, but I'd bet on the low 40s. The rain holds off until evening. It begins around 7 or 8, turns steady by 10, and runs until about 3 in the morning. Expect roughly half an inch to three quarters, with temperatures climbing from the low 30s into the upper 30s overnight.

The forecasters think any ice stays up in the hills, so in Burlington this is mainly a rain event. Still, with holiday travel, watch for a slick spot early in the evening. Friday stays cloudy with showers and a high near 47. Do your driving and walking Thursday before dinner, and keep the umbrella by the door.

week.blurb: Partly cloudy and cold tonight, dropping to around 23, so expect frost on the windshield first thing tomorrow.
Dry and mostly cloudy for Thanksgiving with a high near 42, then steady rain arrives Thursday night, up to three quarters of an inch.
A wet Friday, with rain early and showers the rest of the day, a high near 47 and up to half an inch; bring the umbrella.
Cloudy with a high near 46 and only spotty showers possible, so most of Saturday looks fairly dry.
Looks like the nicest day of the stretch, partly sunny and near 50, with rain holding off until after midnight.
Rain likely Monday with a high near 50, then turning colder tonight, with a low around 31 as it clears out.
Cooler Tuesday, partly sunny with a high near 43, then a chilly night in the upper 20s.
Looks quiet again Wednesday, partly sunny with a high around 44, a touch warmer than Tuesday.

AFD KEY MESSAGES (forecaster's reasoning, issued 2026-11-25T23:19:00+00:00 — covers the whole BTV area, northern NY included: translate to what Burlington feels, never repeat other regions' place names):
  1. Pockets of freezing rain across northern New York and central and northeastern Vermont may cause slippery travel Thanksgiving evening and overnight.
  2. Isolated to scattered power outages near the western slopes of the central and southern Greens are possible associated with strong east winds.
  3. Next chance for precipitation will come Sunday night into Monday as a frontal system crosses our region.
AFD WHAT CHANGED (same regional caveat): As of 237 PM EST Wednesday... A Wind Advisory and a Winter Weather Advisory have been issued for the Thanksgiving evening and overnight hours for portions of the region.
AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: A potent and large low pressure system will track northward from interior North Carolina into western Pennsylvania on Thanksgiving Day. We are dodging a bullet with regards to this storm track, which could have resulted in more widespread and greater amounts of freezing rain; because high pressure will be retreating there will be only marginally cold air to support wintry weather. Given holiday travel, caution will be advised for slippery spots given lack of treatment in this early season. While a Winter Weather Advisory has been issued from tomorrow at 4 PM through Friday at 7 AM, we think the impacts for this event will be on the lower side. One mitigating factor against more widespread impact are expected road temperatures primarily in the middle 30s, consistent with recent warmth and sunshine along with air temperatures barely falling below freezing in areas that see ice accumulations. Also, forecast soundings show the wedge of sub-freezing air will be too shallow for any other precipitation type besides freezing rain (no risk of sleet/snow), and the depth of this layer favors ice accretion primarily above 1500 feet in most areas. Strong easterly winds near the surface overnight, which are discussed in Key Message 2, also should lead to eventual erosion of this sub-freezing layer in areas along and west of higher terrain. In contrast, areas upwind such as near Route 100 in central Vermont will see more persistent cold air result in a more likely ice accumulation. In northern New York, stronger northeasterly flow in the St. Lawrence Valley will also support a greater chance of sub-freezing temperatures being more persistent and accordingly, some ice accretion on untreated surfaces. Conditions should improve by Friday morning due to combination of steady rain ending and continued warming. KEY MESSAGE 2: Strong easterly winds continue to be of some concern, particularly in areas immediately downslope of the Green Mountains in central and southern Vermont where a Wind Advisory is now in effect. The timeframe of strongest winds is tricky, but there is very good consensus that the low level jet will become situated below inversion height and high resolution guidance shows a localized, favorably sharp west-east pressure gradient developing in pressure fields towards 10 PM, concurrent with a 70 knot east- southeast wind field in the 875 to 925 millibar layer just above a shallow low level inversion. Cross sections show some mountain wave breaking, which would be expected to extend only a short distance from our mountain peaks. Therefore, the potential for damaging winds currently looks isolated to the more immediate western slopes. This threat of localized 55 MPH gusts is favored towards our southern areas; the orientation of the spine of the Greens relative to wind direction north of Camel's Hump, along with a weakening jet, makes the threat lower farther north. WCAX METEOROLOGIST (regional station — Burlington relevance only, never their branding): BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) -Happy Wednesday! The busy travel day today ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday looks quiet and a bit warmer with temperatures in the mid to upper 30s and lower 40s for Wednesday afternoon. The day features a good deal of sunshine. Black Friday will see any mountain mixed precipitation transition into mainly rain, and rain could be heavier at times, especially through the morning hours and becoming a bit more scattered by Friday evening and night. The other big component to this system looks to be the wind. That is why we have gone ahead and issued a First Alert Weather Day for Friday. The real bullseye for the wind will be right along the western slopes of the mountains, where they could see gusts upwards of 40-60 MPH. This could be enough to result in scattered power outages Friday. Intensity will vary widely over short distances. Ridgelines and communities on or near the western mountain slopes again could see a window of gusts as high as 40 to 60 mph early Friday. Conditions have to come together in the right way to see the higher end gusts make it to the ground. We usually see wind gusts intensify when rain slows down or stops. Gusts will be much less intense away from the western slopes. Some areas won’t see much wind at all. The strongest gusts will likely occur early Friday morning, especially if there is a lull in precipitation. Wind will trend lighter through the morning and into Friday afternoon. Saturday looks drier overall, but there could still be a few scattered showers and mountain snow showers from time to time. Temperatures are again in the low to mid 40s. Winds look to be calmer through the day Saturday. By Sunday, most of us are back to dry, but cloudy conditions as temperatures continue to warm by a few degrees and we head back towards the mid and upper 40s and lower 50s.
NBC5 METEOROLOGIST (2026-11-25T23:35:00Z — same caveat): Rain, ice, wind late on Thanksgiving — Thanksgiving starts dry, with some sun, before clouds thicken up by afternoon. A coastal low sends in steady rain by evening and overnight, which may start as an icy mix in the mountains. Highs reach the low 40s. Strong downslope wind will cause issues Thursday night into Friday morning. Bennington County is where the most outages will be, with 70 mph gust potential. Some will also occur in eastern Rutland and Addison counties. By daytime Friday, less wind. Expect a cloudy sky with scattered rain showers through the morning and afternoon. A few snowflakes may mix in for the mountains, especially late. This weekend brings lingering showers of rain and mountain snow (especially Saturday), lots of clouds and a mild feel. Highs reach the 40s to around 50. More sun by Sunday.
